questions.stem: In myocardium reperfusion injury is due to?
questions.solutionHtml: of the Incorrect Options: (B) Mg (Magnesium): Magnesium is not a primary factor in reperfusion injury. In fact, magnesium often has a protective role in cardiac cells by stabilizing ion channels, reducing calcium overload, and minimizing oxidative stress. Its deficiency can exacerbate ischemia-reperfusion injury, but magnesium itself is not a causative agent. (C) K (Potassium): Potassium levels are disrupted during ischemia and reperfusion, but they are not the primary cause of reperfusion injury. Abnormal potassium handling can lead to arrhythmias, but it does not directly result in the cellular damage seen in reperfusion injury. Potassium imbalances are more of a consequence than a cause in this context. (D) Mn (Manganese): Manganese is a trace element that has antioxidant properties and is a component of the enzyme manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD), which helps mitigate oxidative stress. It is not involved in the pathogenesis of reperfusion injury but may play a protective role against oxidative damage.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a sign of reversible cell injury?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) Option A- ATP depletion is one of the earliest biochemical changes occurring in cell injury Option B- Feature of apoptosis (cell death, not reversible cell injury) Option C- Cellular swelling and fatty change are earliest findings of reversible cell injury Option D- Depletion of ATP is a consequence of reduced phosphorylation

questions.stem: For programmed cell death and autopagy, which is pro apoptotic genes?
questions.solutionHtml: of the Incorrect Options: (A) BCL2: BCL2 is an anti-apoptotic gene that inhibits apoptosis by stabilizing the mitochondrial membrane and preventing the release of cytochrome c. It counteracts pro-apoptotic proteins like BAX and promotes cell survival. Thus, it is not pro-apoptotic but rather a key regulator in preventing apoptosis. (C) BCL-XL: Like BCL2, BCL-XL is an anti-apoptotic member of the Bcl-2 family. It binds to and inhibits pro-apoptotic proteins, such as BAX and BAK, preventing them from compromising mitochondrial integrity. Its function is to promote cell survival rather than apoptosis. (D) BIM: BIM is a pro-apoptotic BH3-only protein, but it acts indirectly. It promotes apoptosis by binding to and neutralizing anti-apoptotic proteins like BCL2 and BCL-XL, allowing pro-apoptotic proteins like BAX and BAK to function. While BIM plays a role in apoptosis, it is not the direct mediator like BAX, which directly disrupts mitochondrial membranes.

questions.stem: The p53 gene, a tumour suppressor gene, plays a crucial role in
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) p53 detects DNA damage and triggers programmed cell death (apoptosis) to prevent the propagation of defective cells. Other options: A) Promoting uncontrolled cell division: The p53 gene functions to suppress tumors and does the opposite by preventing uncontrolled cell division C) Preventing DNA repair mechanisms: p53 promotes DNA repair mechanisms when damage is detected, allowing the cell to restore its integrity before dividing D) Inhibiting cell cycle arrest: p53 induces cell cycle arrest at the G1/S checkpoint to give the cell time to repair DNA damage or undergo apoptosis

questions.stem: True about caspases are?

options.label: D
options.text: They are proteases which cause cellular death in apoptosis

questions.answerText: They are proteases which cause cellular death in apoptosis
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) Best option here is option D. Caspases are not the first enzymes activated in apoptosis but they are cysteine proteases involved in protein breakdown leading to apoptosis

questions.stem: True about necroptosis is all except?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) Option A- feature of pyroptosis Option B- caspase independent programmed cell death Option C- after death receptor interaction failure to activate caspase 8 can lead to activation of necroptosis Option D- free radical damage is a part of the mechanism of cell death by necroptosis

questions.stem: SMAC/DIAMBLO is a:

options.label: C
options.text: Acts both as anti and pro apoptotic protein

questions.solutionHtml: of the Incorrect Options: (A) Anti-apoptotic protein: SMAC/DIABLO is not anti-apoptotic. Its role is to promote apoptosis by antagonizing anti-apoptotic IAPs. Anti-apoptotic proteins, such as BCL-2 or BCL-XL, work to preserve cell survival by inhibiting pro-apoptotic pathways. SMAC/DIABLO works in opposition to these types of proteins. (B) Induces necrosis: SMAC/DIABLO does not induce necrosis, which is an uncontrolled and non-programmed form of cell death characterized by inflammation and cell rupture. SMAC/DIABLO specifically facilitates programmed cell death (apoptosis) by enhancing caspase activity. It is not associated with necrotic pathways. (C) Acts both as anti- and pro-apoptotic protein: SMAC/DIABLO is strictly a pro-apoptotic protein. It does not have a dual role as both anti- and pro-apoptotic. Its function is solely to promote apoptosis by inhibiting IAPs and enabling caspase activation. Proteins like BCL-2 family members may exhibit dual roles in apoptosis, but SMAC/DIABLO does not.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an execution caspase:
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) Caspase 3, 6 and 7 are execution caspases Caspase 8 is an initiator caspase of extrinsic pathway Caspase 9 is an initiator caspase of intrinsic pathway

questions.stem: Annexin V is a marker of-
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) Annexin V is a hallmark marker for early apoptosis due to its ability to detect phosphatidylserine translocation Other options: Necrosis: In necrosis, there is uncontrolled cell death with membrane rupture, and Annexin V does not bind as phosphatidylserine remains buried until the membrane disintegrates Gangrene: Gangrene is a macroscopic tissue death caused by infection or lack of blood supply and is not specifically associated with phosphatidylserine exposure Aging: While aging cells may eventually undergo apoptosis, Annexin V specifically marks apoptotic events, not the general process of cellular aging

questions.stem: The following is not a sensor of apoptosis:
questions.solutionHtml: on of the Incorrect Options: (A) Puma: Puma (p53-upregulated modulator of apoptosis) is a BH3-only protein and a sensor of apoptotic signals. It is transcriptionally upregulated by p53 in response to cellular stress, such as DNA damage, and functions by neutralizing anti-apoptotic proteins like BCL-2 and BCL-XL. This allows pro-apoptotic effectors like BAX and BAK to initiate mitochondrial permeabilization and trigger apoptosis. Thus, Puma acts as a sensor of apoptotic signals, not an effector. (B) Noxa: Noxa is another BH3-only protein and sensor of apoptosis, activated in response to stress signals mediated by p53. Like Puma, Noxa binds to and inhibits anti-apoptotic proteins, facilitating the activation of BAX and BAK. Its role is upstream, sensing cellular stress and helping to commit the cell to apoptosis, classifying it as a sensor. (D) BAD: BAD (Bcl-2-associated death promoter) is also a BH3-only sensor protein. It promotes apoptosis by binding to and inhibiting anti-apoptotic proteins, such as BCL-2 and BCL-XL, thereby releasing pro-apoptotic effectors like BAX and BAK. BAD is activated by dephosphorylation and functions as a sensor of apoptotic signals, not as a direct effector.

questions.stem: Intrinsic pathway of apoptosis is initiated by all the following except:
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) Type 1 TNF receptor (TNFR1) activates the extrinsic pathway of apoptosis by binding to tumour necrosis factor (TNF), which leads to the recruitment of death-inducing signalling complex (DISC) and caspase-8 activation Other options: Growth factor withdrawal: Withdrawal of growth factors can lead to mitochondrial dysfunction, cytochrome c release, and activation of the intrinsic pathway DNA damage: DNA damage activates the intrinsic pathway through p53-mediated signalling, leading to mitochondrial permeabilization Protein misfolding: Accumulation of misfolded proteins induces endoplasmic reticulum stress, which can trigger the intrinsic apoptotic pathway

questions.stem: Defective apoptosis and increased cell survival is seen in:
questions.solutionHtml: n of the Incorrect Options: (B) Neurodegenerative diseases: Neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and Huntington's disease, are associated with excessive apoptosis rather than defective apoptosis. In these conditions, neuronal cells undergo premature and uncontrolled apoptosis, leading to progressive loss of neurons and functional deficits. These diseases are linked to increased apoptosis, not increased cell survival, making this option incorrect. (C) Viral infections: In some viral infections, apoptosis may be inhibited as viruses develop strategies to evade the host immune system by blocking apoptotic pathways (e.g., using viral proteins to inhibit caspases or anti-apoptotic proteins). However, this phenomenon is context-specific and not a generalized cause of defective apoptosis leading to increased cell survival. Furthermore, in many cases, apoptosis is actually triggered to eliminate infected cells, so this option is less relevant than autoimmune diseases. (D) Ischemic injury: Ischemic injury, such as myocardial infarction or stroke, is primarily associated with excessive cell death, including both necrosis and apoptosis, rather than defective apoptosis or increased cell survival. In these conditions, apoptosis contributes to the damage caused by oxygen deprivation and reperfusion injury, making this option incorrect.

questions.stem: Receptor associated kinases 1 (RIP1) and 3 (RIP3) are involved in:
questions.solutionHtml: n of the Incorrect Options: (A) Necrosis: Necrosis is an uncontrolled and accidental form of cell death caused by severe injury or trauma. It is not regulated and does not involve specific signaling pathways like RIP1 and RIP3. Necrosis leads to the uncontrolled release of cellular contents and inflammation, but it lacks the regulated processes characteristic of necroptosis, making this option incorrect. (B) Apoptosis: Apoptosis is a regulated form of cell death mediated by caspases, which are not involved in necroptosis. RIP1 and RIP3 do not play a central role in apoptosis, as apoptosis relies on distinct signaling pathways such as those involving caspase-3 and caspase-9. Additionally, apoptosis does not result in the inflammatory outcomes seen in necroptosis, further differentiating the two processes. (D) Pyroptosis: Pyroptosis is a regulated inflammatory form of cell death mediated by gasdermin proteins and caspases, particularly caspase-1 and caspase-11 (or their equivalents). It is triggered by the activation of inflammasomes and is associated with the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1? and IL-18. RIP1 and RIP3 are not involved in pyroptosis, making this option incorrect.

questions.stem: Inflammasome is formed in:
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) Microbial products that enter the cytoplasm of infected cells are recognized by cytoplasmic innate immune receptors and can activate the multiprotein complex called the inflammasome. The function of the inflammasome is to activate caspase1, (also known as interleukin-1 Beta converting enzyme) which cleaves a precursor form of IL-1 and releases its biologically active form. IL-1 is a mediator of many aspects of inflammation, including leukocyte recruitment and fever. Caspase-1 and, more importantly, the closely related caspase-11 also induce death of the cells. Unlike classical apoptosis, this pathway of cell death is characterized by swelling of cells, loss of plasma membrane integrity, and release of inflammatory mediators. Pyroptosis results in the death of some microbes that gain access to the cytosol and promotes the release of inflammasome-generated IL-1.

questions.stem: Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in all of the following except:
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) Fibrinoid necrosis is a special form of necrosis usually seen in immune reactions involving blood vessels. This pattern of necrosis typically occurs when complexes of antigens and antibodies are deposited in the walls of arteries. Deposits of these “immune complexes,” together with fibrin that has leaked out of vessels, result in a bright pink and amorphous appearance in H&E stains, called “fibrinoid” (fibrin-like) by pathologists. This pattern of necrosis is seen classically in options A, B and C as well as rejection of transplants.

questions.stem: Organelle where H2O2 is produced and destroyed is:
questions.solutionHtml:
ation of the Correct Answer:

Peroxisomes are specialized organelles involved in the production and detoxification of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). Peroxisomes contain enzymes such as oxidases, which generate H2O2 as a byproduct of various metabolic reactions, including the breakdown of fatty acids and the oxidation of other substrates. To prevent cellular damage from the highly reactive H2O2, peroxisomes also contain the enzyme catalase, which converts H2O2 into water and oxygen. This dual function of producing and detoxifying H2O2 makes peroxisomes critical for cellular homeostasis and protection against oxidative stress.

Explanation of the Incorrect Options:

(B) Lysosome:
Lysosomes are involved in intracellular digestion and the breakdown of macromolecules through hydrolytic enzymes like proteases, lipases, and nucleases. They do not produce or detoxify H2O2. Their primary role is in degrading cellular waste, not managing reactive oxygen species like H2O2, making this option incorrect.

(C) Golgi body:
The Golgi apparatus is responsible for processing, modifying, and packaging proteins and lipids for secretion or transport to other organelles. It is not involved in the production or detoxification of H2O2. Its functions are related to vesicle trafficking and glycosylation, not oxidative metabolism, so this option is incorrect.

(D) Ribosome:
Ribosomes are involved in protein synthesis by translating mRNA into polypeptide chains. They do not participate in the production or detoxification of H2O2. Ribosomes lack any metabolic or enzymatic functions related to oxidative stress management, making this option irrelevant in this context.

questions.stem: Which of these is not responsible for removal of free radicals?
questions.solutionHtml:
ptions:

(A) Catalase:
Catalase is a key enzyme in the detoxification of free radicals. It breaks down hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), a reactive oxygen species, into water and oxygen. This reaction prevents the accumulation of H2O2, which can otherwise generate harmful hydroxyl radicals. As an enzyme involved in free radical detoxification, catalase is not the correct answer.

(B) Superoxide Dismutase (SOD):
Superoxide dismutase (SOD) is an essential antioxidant enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of superoxide radicals (O2-) into hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and oxygen. This reaction is a critical step in the cellular defense against oxidative stress. Like catalase, SOD removes free radicals and is not the correct answer.

(D) Glutathione Peroxidase:
Glutathione peroxidase is another antioxidant enzyme that reduces hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and organic hydroperoxides to water and alcohols, using reduced glutathione as a cofactor. This enzyme plays a significant role in mitigating oxidative stress and removing free radicals, making it an important detoxifier.

questions.stem: In cell death, myelin figures are derived from-
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) Myelin figures are characteristic of necrotic cell death and result from the breakdown of the cell membrane Other options: A) Nucleus: The nucleus does not directly form myelin figures. However, nuclear fragmentation (karyorrhexis) occurs in apoptosis C) Cytoplasm: While myelin figures are found in the cytoplasm, they are derived from the membrane, not the cytoplasm itself D) Mitochondria: Mitochondria are involved in initiating apoptosis but do not directly form myelin figures

questions.stem: The sign of reversible injury in a case of alcoholic liver disease-
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) The presence of cytoplasmic vacuoles (fatty changes or hydropic changes) indicates reversible injury, as the cells are undergoing a non-lethal stress response Other options: A) Loss of cell membrane: Loss of the cell membrane is a feature of irreversible injury, leading to cell rupture and necrosis B) Nuclear karyolysis: Karyolysis refers to the dissolution of the nucleus, a sign of irreversible cell injury and necrosis D) Pyknosis: Pyknosis is the condensation of the nucleus and is a sign of irreversible injury, commonly associated with apoptosis or necrosis

questions.stem: Irreversible cell injury is indicated by-
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) Influx of calcium into mitochondria increases its permeability thus causing a cascade of changes responsible for cellular death. Myelin figures can be seen in both reversible and irreversible Injury however accumulation of calcium of mitochondria is a lethal change characteristic of irreversible cell injury

questions.stem: Type of necrosis occurring in brain-
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Answer (B)
Enzymatic digestion by both enzymes released from dying cells and inflammatory cells causes lysis of the dead cells into a liquefied viscous mass- liquefactive necrosis. 
Option A- Most common pattern of ischemic necrosis in all organs other than brain
Option C- Usually in vasculitis 
Option D- Central necrosis leading to cheese like necrosis on gross

questions.stem: Which of the following organs shows fat necrosis?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) The pancreas is known for fat necrosis, especially in cases of acute pancreatitis. In pancreatitis, the release of pancreatic enzymes (lipases) leads to the breakdown of fat, forming chalky, white deposits in the tissue, which is a classic feature of fat necrosis Other options: A) Liver: The liver is more prone to fatty change (steatosis) but does not commonly exhibit fat necrosis. Fat necrosis occurs in tissues with high fat content, especially after trauma or inflammation. C) Kidney: The kidney does not commonly show fat necrosis. It may experience other forms of damage, but fat necrosis is not characteristic D) Heart: The heart can suffer from conditions like infarction or myocardial injury, but fat necrosis is not typical

questions.stem: Example of apoptosis is-
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) Option B-Calcified bodies seen in congestive splenomegaly Option C-Intracytoplasmic accumulation of Igs in plasma cells (seen in multiple myeloma) Option D-Intranuclear inclusions seen in multiple myeloma

questions.stem: Characteristic feature of apoptosis-
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) Chromatin condensation is a key feature of apoptosis. The chromatin in the nucleus condenses and compacts, often forming dense clumps, which is a hallmark of apoptotic cell death Other options: During apoptosis, the cell membrane remains intact initially, but it can later exhibit blebbing, although the integrity of the membrane is largely maintained compared to necrosis Cytoplasmic eosinophilia is typically associated with necrosis, not apoptosis. In apoptosis, cytoplasm remains normal or may become slightly more condensed Cell shrinkage is also characteristic of apoptosis. The cell undergoes a reduction in size, a process that contrasts with necrosis, where the cell swells due to loss of membrane integrity

questions.stem: A 55-years-old male who has a long history of excessive drinking presents with signs of alcoholic hepatitis. Microscopic Examination of a biopsy of this patient’s liver reveals irregular eosinophilic hyaline inclusions within the cytoplasm of the hepatocytes. These eosinophilic inclusions are composed of:
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) In alcoholic hepatitis, the eosinophilic hyaline inclusions seen in hepatocytes are Mallory bodies, which are composed of keratin intermediate filaments Other options: A) Immunoglobulins: Immunoglobulins can accumulate in certain conditions (like in chronic liver disease or cirrhosis), they are not the primary components of Mallory bodies B) Excess of plasma protein: While plasma proteins like fibrinogen or albumin can accumulate in certain liver conditions, Mallory bodies are not made of plasma proteins but of keratin filaments D) Lipofuscin: Lipofuscin is a pigment of aging and oxidative stress, often seen in cells as brownish granules, but it is not associated with the eosinophilic hyaline inclusions in alcoholic hepatitis

questions.stem: Lipofuscin granules are examples of
questions.solutionHtml: n of the Incorrect Options: (A) Apoptotic bodies: Apoptotic bodies are membrane-bound vesicles that form during apoptosis, containing cellular fragments such as nuclear material and cytoplasm. They are phagocytosed and removed by neighboring cells or macrophages. Lipofuscin granules are not associated with apoptosis or apoptotic bodies; they result from long-term metabolic activity rather than cell death, making this option incorrect. (C) Psammomatous calcification: Psammomatous calcification refers to concentric, lamellated calcified structures, often seen in certain tumors like papillary thyroid carcinoma or meningioma. These calcifications have a different origin and structure compared to lipofuscin granules, which do not involve calcification or the deposition of calcium salts. Thus, this option is incorrect. (D) Hyaline change: Hyaline change describes the accumulation of homogenous, glassy, eosinophilic material in cells or tissues, often composed of proteins. Examples include hyaline arteriolosclerosis and intracellular hyaline droplets. Lipofuscin granules are pigmented and granular, not homogenous or proteinaceous like hyaline changes, making this option incorrect.

questions.stem: All of the following are true about apoptosis except
questions.solutionHtml: n of the Incorrect Options: (A) Cell shrinkage: Cell shrinkage is a hallmark of apoptosis. During apoptosis, the cell decreases in size as its cytoplasm condenses and organelles become tightly packed. This is a distinct feature of apoptosis that differentiates it from necrosis, where cells typically swell and rupture. Thus, this statement is correct and not an exception. (B) Altered orientation of lipids: Apoptosis involves the externalization of phosphatidylserine, a lipid normally confined to the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane. This alteration in lipid orientation acts as an "eat-me" signal, facilitating the recognition and phagocytosis of apoptotic cells by macrophages. This feature is a well-documented aspect of apoptosis, making this statement correct. (D) No adjacent inflammation: Apoptosis is a controlled and non-inflammatory process because apoptotic bodies are neatly packaged and phagocytosed without releasing cellular contents into the surrounding environment. This prevents the activation of inflammatory responses, distinguishing apoptosis from necrosis, which triggers inflammation. Therefore, this statement is accurate and not an exception.

questions.stem: Which of the following is/are true about the microscopic appearance of necrotic cells?

options.label: A
options.text: Increased eosinophilia due to loss of cytoplasmic RNA

options.label: B
options.text: Increased eosinophilia due to denaturation of cytoplasmic proteins

options.label: C
options.text: Glassy homogenous appearance due to loss of glycogen particles

questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) Necrotic cells show increased eosinophilia in hematoxylin and eosin (H & E) stains, attributable in part to the loss of cytoplasmic RNA (which binds the blue dye, hematoxylin) and in part to denatured cytoplasmic proteins (which bind the red dye, eosin). The necrotic cell may have a more glassy homogeneous appearance than do normal cells, mainly as a result of the loss of glycogen particles. When enzymes have digested the cytoplasmic organelles, the cytoplasm becomes vacuolated and appears moth-eaten.

questions.stem: Which phenomenon/phenomena characterise irreversibility of cell injury?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) Two phenomena consistently characterize irreversibility—the inability to reverse mitochondrial dysfunction (lack of oxidative phosphorylation and ATP generation) even after resolution of the original injury and profound disturbances in membrane function. Injury to lysosomal membranes results in the enzymatic dis-solution of the injured cell that is characteristic of necrosis.

questions.stem: All of the following is/are true about extrinsic pathway of apoptosis except

options.label: A
options.text: Engagement of plasma membrane death receptors

options.label: B
options.text: Type I TNF receptor is prototype

options.label: D
options.text: Mechanism of apoptosis of virus infected cells

questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) In the extrinsic pathway of apoptosis, caspase-8 is the initiator caspase, not caspase-9, which is classically involved in the intrinsic pathway Other options: Engagement of plasma membrane death receptors: The extrinsic pathway of apoptosis is initiated by the engagement of death receptors (such as TNF receptors or Fas receptors) on the plasma membrane. This triggers the apoptotic signalling cascade Type 1 TNF receptor is prototype: The Type 1 TNF receptor (TNFR1) is a prototype of death receptors in the extrinsic pathway. Binding of TNF to this receptor leads to the formation of the death-inducing signalling complex (DISC) and activation of caspase-8 Mechanism of apoptosis in virus-infected cells: While the intrinsic pathway is more commonly associated with apoptosis in virus-infected cells, the extrinsic pathway can also be activated, particularly through Fas ligand binding to Fas receptor, to induce apoptosis in response to viral infection

questions.stem: Programmed necrosis is another name for
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) The following features characterize necroptosis: Morphologically, and to some extent biochemically, it resembles necrosis, both characterized by loss of ATP, swelling of the cell and organelles, generation of ROS, release of lysosomal enzymes and ultimately rupture of the plasma membrane as discussed earlier. Mechanistically, it is triggered by genetically programmed signal transduction events that culminate in cell death. In this respect it resembles programmed cell death, which is considered the hallmark of apoptosis Because of the duality of these features, necroptosis is sometimes called programmed necrosis to distinguish it from the more usual forms of necrosis driven passively by toxic or anoxic injury to the cell. In sharp contrast to apoptosis, the genetic program that drives necroptosis does not result in caspase activation and hence it is also sometimes referred to as “caspase-independent” programmed cell death.

questions.stem: Macrophage-specific deletion of which autophagy related gene increases susceptibility to tuberculosis
questions.solutionHtml: n of the Incorrect Options: (A) Atg 3: Atg3 is an E2-like enzyme involved in the conjugation of Atg8 (LC3) to phosphatidylethanolamine, a critical step in autophagosome formation. While Atg3 is important for autophagy, its macrophage-specific deletion has not been directly linked to increased susceptibility to tuberculosis. This makes it a less relevant option compared to Atg5. (B) Atg 4: Atg4 is a cysteine protease that processes Atg8 (LC3) precursors, allowing them to participate in autophagosome formation. While Atg4 is essential for general autophagy, studies have not identified its macrophage-specific deletion as a direct factor in increased susceptibility to tuberculosis. Therefore, it is not the correct choice. (D) Atg 6: Atg6 is another name for Beclin-1, a key regulator of autophagy. While Beclin-1 is critical for initiating autophagy, its specific role in macrophage-related resistance to tuberculosis has not been emphasized to the same extent as Atg5. Additionally, the question specifically refers to the susceptibility linked to Atg5 deletion, not Beclin-1.

questions.stem: Immune complexes mediated necrosis is of which type?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) Fibrinoid necrosis is the type of necrosis associated with immune complex deposition, commonly seen in autoimmune diseases and in small blood vessels Other options: A) Coagulative: Coagulative necrosis typically occurs in solid organs like the heart or kidneys due to ischemic injury (e.g., myocardial infarction). It is characterized by the preservation of tissue architecture for a while, but with loss of cellular details B) Liquefactive: Liquefactive necrosis occurs in the brain (e.g., cerebral infarction) and in abscesses, where tissue is digested into a liquid form due to enzymatic action C) Caseous: Caseous necrosis is often associated with tuberculosis, where the tissue has a cheese-like appearance due to the formation of granulomas

questions.stem: All are reversible injury of cell, except-
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) Karyorrhexis (fragmentation of the nucleus) is a sign of irreversible injury and is often associated with necrosis. Once the nucleus undergoes karyorrhexis, the damage is too severe for the cell to recover Other options: A) Vacuole: Vacuolization of the cytoplasm is a feature of reversible injury. It occurs due to water accumulation (hydropic change) or fat accumulation in the cell but can reverse once the stress is removed C) Fat accumulation: Fat accumulation (fatty change) is a reversible injury. It occurs due to metabolic disturbances, like alcohol consumption or diabetes, and can be reversed if the underlying cause is addressed D) Cell wall swelling: Swelling of the cell (or cell membrane) is another indicator of reversible injury. It is typically caused by ionic disturbances or water accumulation and can return to normal once the stressor is removed

questions.stem: Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in following except-
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) Diabetes mellitus is associated with hyaline arteriosclerosis (not fibrinoid necrosis) due to chronic high blood sugar levels. It causes thickening and narrowing of the blood vessel walls, but fibrinoid necrosis is not typically seen in this condition Other options: A) PAN (Polyarteritis nodosa) is a systemic vasculitis that involves small- to medium-sized arteries and is commonly associated with fibrinoid necrosis in the vessel walls C) Malignant hypertension can lead to fibrinoid necrosis in the blood vessel walls, especially in the kidneys, as a result of extremely high blood pressure causing damage to the vascular endothelium D) SLE (Systemic lupus erythematosus) is an autoimmune disease that can cause fibrinoid necrosis in various tissues, particularly in blood vessels, due to immune complex deposition

questions.stem: CD-95 is a marker of-
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) CD95 (Fas) is a death receptor, involved in the extrinsic apoptotic pathway. Its activation by FasL triggers programmed cell death Other options: B) MHC complex is involved in antigen presentation but is not related to CD95 C) T helper cells: While CD95 is expressed on many cell types, it is not specific to T helper cells. T helper cells are often identified by CD4 markers, not CD95 D) NK cells can express CD95, but CD95 itself is not a defining marker of NK cells. NK cells are more commonly identified by CD56 or CD16 markers

questions.stem: True about apoptosis is-
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) Apoptosis is an energy-dependent process that requires ATP to activate and regulate the cascade of events leading to cell death. It involves the activation of caspases and other proteins that require energy for proper function Other options: Apoptosis can be self-initiated through intrinsic pathways (like mitochondrial involvement) or triggered by external signals. Both pathways lead to activation of caspases and other apoptotic machinery Swelling of the cytoplasm is a feature of necrosis, not apoptosis. In apoptosis, the cell typically shrinks and undergoes fragmentation without cytoplasmic swelling In apoptosis, the cell membrane remains largely intact during the early stages. It is the cell's contents that are contained within vesicles, avoiding inflammation. Loss of membrane integrity occurs in necrosis

questions.stem: Which of the following organelles plays a pivotal role in apoptosis?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) Mitochondria play a pivotal role in apoptosis by releasing pro-apoptotic factors such as cytochrome c, which activate the caspase cascade leading to programmed cell death Other options: B) Endoplasmic reticulum is involved in stress responses but is not as central to the apoptosis process as mitochondria. ER stress can lead to apoptosis in some cases, but mitochondria play a more direct role in the execution phase of apoptosis C) Nucleus contains the genetic material and undergoes changes during apoptosis (like chromatin condensation and fragmentation), but it is not the central organelle responsible for initiating the apoptotic process D) Golgi apparatus is responsible for processing and sorting proteins but does not play a direct role in the initiation or execution of apoptosis

questions.stem: Cytosolic cytochrome C plays an important function in-
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) Cytosolic cytochrome C plays a crucial role in apoptosis. During apoptosis, cytochrome C is released from the mitochondria into the cytosol, where it activates caspase-9 to initiate the apoptotic cascade, leading to cell death Other options: Cytochrome C is not involved in cell necrosis. Necrosis is a form of uncontrolled cell death typically caused by external factors like trauma or toxins, and it does not involve the caspase-dependent apoptotic pathway in which cytochrome C is involved Cytochrome C is involved in the electron transport chain in mitochondria, but in this context, it is not cytosolic. It facilitates electron transfer between Complex III and Complex IV, playing a role in ATP production, but this is separate from its role in apoptosis Cytosolic cytochrome C is not directly involved in cell division. Cell division is regulated by other mechanisms, such as the cell cycle machinery and checkpoint proteins

questions.stem: In apoptosis, cytochrome C acts through
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) In apoptosis, cytochrome C is released from the mitochondria into the cytosol, where it binds to Apaf-1 (Apoptotic Protease Activating Factor-1). This binding activates Apaf-1 and leads to the formation of the apoptosome, which in turn activates caspase-9. Caspase-9 initiates a cascade of caspase activation that leads to programmed cell death Other options: BCL-2 is an anti-apoptotic protein that regulates mitochondrial outer membrane permeability, preventing cytochrome C release. It does not directly mediate cytochrome C's function in apoptosis FADD (Fas-associated death domain) is involved in the extrinsic apoptotic pathway, typically in response to death receptor signalling. It does not directly interact with cytochrome C TNF is involved in the extrinsic apoptosis pathway by binding to death receptors, leading to the activation of caspases through FADD. It does not directly interact with cytochrome C

questions.stem: Which of the following has a direct role in apoptosis-
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) Cytochrome C plays a direct and crucial role in apoptosis. It is released from mitochondria into the cytoplasm in response to apoptotic signals and activates caspase-9, initiating the caspase cascade that leads to programmed cell death Other options: Nitric oxide can modulate various cellular processes, including apoptosis, but it does not have a direct, central role in the apoptotic pathway itself. Its role in apoptosis is more indirect, often involved in signalling pathways that can either promote or inhibit cell death Adenyl cyclase is an enzyme that synthesizes cAMP, but it does not have a direct role in apoptosis. cAMP and adenyl cyclase are more involved in various signalling pathways, such as those controlling cell proliferation and survival cAMP is a second messenger that primarily regulates various cellular processes, including cell growth and metabolism. While it can influence apoptosis indirectly through signalling pathways, it does not have a direct role in the execution of apoptosis

questions.stem: Which of the following pigments are involved in free radical injury?
questions.solutionHtml: n of the Incorrect Options: (B) Melanin: Melanin is a pigment involved in the protection of tissues from UV radiation and does not play a role in free radical injury. It serves an antioxidant function by scavenging free radicals generated by UV exposure, rather than being a byproduct of free radical damage. Hence, it is not associated with free radical injury in the same way as lipofuscin. (C) Bilirubin: Bilirubin is a breakdown product of heme metabolism and is primarily involved in the excretion of waste products from red blood cell turnover. While bilirubin has mild antioxidant properties and may scavenge free radicals, it is not a pigment formed as a direct consequence of free radical injury. Its accumulation is related to conditions like jaundice, not oxidative stress. (D) Hematin: Hematin is a pigment derived from hemoglobin breakdown, often seen in conditions involving hemolysis or parasitic infections (e.g., malaria). It is not formed due to free radical injury and has no significant association with oxidative stress or lipid peroxidation, making it an incorrect choice.

questions.stem: Which finding on electron microscopy indicates irreversible cell injury -

options.label: B
options.text: Dissociation of ribosomes from rough endoplasmic reticulum

options.label: C
options.text: Flocculent amorphous densities in the mitochondria

questions.answerText: Flocculent amorphous densities in the mitochondria
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) The presence of flocculent, amorphous densities in the mitochondria is characteristic of irreversible injury. It signifies mitochondrial dysfunction, a critical feature of irreversible cell injury, and often precedes cell death Other options: A) Dilatation of endoplasmic reticulum: Dilatation of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a sign of reversible cell injury. It reflects cellular stress but can be reversed if the stressor is removed B) Dissociation of ribosomes from rough endoplasmic reticulum: Dissociation of ribosomes from the rough ER is also associated with reversible injury. This process can occur when cells are under stress but can recover if the stress is eliminated D) Myelin figures: Myelin figures can be seen in both reversible and irreversible injury, but they are more commonly associated with irreversible injury. However, they are not as definitive a marker as the mitochondrial changes described above

questions.stem: MI is a type of-
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) Coagulative necrosis is the hallmark of tissue damage in myocardial infarction. It preserves the tissue architecture for a short period after the injury, while cellular details are lost due to the denaturation of proteins Other options: B) Liquefactive: Liquefactive necrosis occurs when the tissue is digested by enzymes, leading to the formation of a liquid mass. It is often seen in brain tissue or abscesses, but not in myocardial infarction C) Caseous: Caseous necrosis is characterized by a cheese-like appearance and is most commonly seen in tuberculosis or certain fungal infections, not in myocardial infarction D) Fat: Fat necrosis typically occurs in adipose tissue, often after trauma or in pancreatic injury (like acute pancreatitis), and is not associated with myocardial infarction

questions.stem: Pyogenic bacterial infections and ischemic brain infarcts most characteristically produce which one of the listed types of necrosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Answer (D)
Liquefactive necrosis- is the type of necrosis produced by acute bacterial infections. With liquefactive necrosis the dead cells are completely dissolved by hydrolytic enzymes from acute inflammatory cells and all that remains is a liquid mass.
Liquefactive necrosis can also be seen with fungal infections, and it is the type of necrosis that is produced by ischemic necrosis of the brain.

questions.stem: Reversible cell injury is characterized by which of the following changes?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) Cellular swelling Reversible injury to cells is characterized by a reduction in energy stores (ATP) and changes in ion concentrations, resulting in water influx. Morphologically, this is demonstrated by cellular swelling, microscopic vacuoles, and lipid vacuoles. Eventually, sufficient cellular injury occurs such that the damage becomes irreversible, resulting in cell death by either necrosis or apoptosis. Irreversible changes of injury resulting in necrosis are characterized by cell membrane disruption, lysosomal rupture, and severe mitochondrial damage. Apoptosis is a form of cell death that is more controlled and results in nuclear dissolution (karyorrhexis) and cell fragmentation without loss of membrane integrity.

questions.stemHtml: An atherosclerotic plaque ruptures and obstructs blood flow to a segment of kidney. At 6 hours after the event, the involved kidney would show what pattern of necrosis on microscopic examination?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) Coagulative necrosis Coagulative necrosis most often occurs when an interruption in blood supply results in tissue ischemia and death. This pattern of necrosis preserves the tissue architecture for several days, but the cells are eosinophilic and lack nuclei. Liquefactive necrosis is characterized by digestion of the dead cells, resulting in a liquid, viscous mass; this pattern is frequently seen in bacterial infections and CNS infarction. Gangrenous necrosis refers to cell death, typically in a limb, which has superimposed infection. Caseous necrosis is most common in tuberculous infection, resulting in cheese-like white friable material. Fibrinoid necrosis is a special form of necrosis around vessels where immune complexes are deposited, resulting in a “bright pink” amorphous appearance.

questions.stem: All of the following statements about apoptosis are true except?

options.label: A
options.text: Apoptosis is an integral part of embryogenesis

options.label: B
options.text: Appears as cell fragments with intact cytoplasmic membranes

options.label: C
options.text: Can be activated by FAS-FAS ligand binding

questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) Incites a brisk inflammatory response Apoptosis is a pathway of cell death caused by a tightly regulated cell suicide program, which can be mediated internally due to release of certain proteins, and externally through membrane receptors, most notably FAS and FAS-ligand. It is a normal component of many cellular processes, including germinal centers and embryogenesis. Morphologically, it is characterized by cell fragmentation but maintenance of cellular membranes prevents an inflammatory response.

questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old woman undergoes an endomyocardial biopsy that is shown in Figure 3-4. The histochemical stain of choice is?
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Answer (A)

Congo red

The figure depicts amorphous, eosinophilic extracellular amyloid deposits. Although trichrome and PAS stain amyloid deposits gray-blue and magenta, respectively, Congo red stain imparts a characteristic orange-red color to the deposits. In addition, it has the unique ability to intercalate with the β-pleated structure, and produce an apple-green birefringence upon polarization. Cardiac amyloidosis (stiff heart syndrome) presents as restrictive cardiomyopathy and usually occurs as a complication of primary amyloidosis with AL (light chain) protein deposition.

questions.stem: A myocardial infarct marked by a prominent neutrophilic component and coagulative necrosis with loss of myocyte nuclei and striation is approximately how old?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) 2 days Coagulation necrosis with loss of myocyte nuclei and striations and a prominent neutrophilic interstitial infiltrate is generally encountered in a myocardial infarct of 1–3 days age.  At 12 hours, early evidence of coagulation necrosis with edema and hemorrhage may be seen. At 24 hours, pyknosis with myocyte hypereosinophilia, marginal contraction band necrosis, and early neutrophilic infiltrate may be evident. At 5 days, early disintegration of dead muscle fibers with dying neutrophils and early macrophage infiltrate may be evident. At 7 days, macrophages predominate and the early development of granulation tissue at the margin of the infarct may be evident.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman presents with fever, chills, headache, neck stiffness, vomiting, and confusion.The Kernig sign and Brudzinski sign are both positive.Examination of the CSF reveals changes consistent with bacterial meningitis, and brain imaging demonstrates a localized abscess.Which of the following types of necrosis is most characteristic of abscess formation?
questions.solutionHtml: n for the Incorrect Options: A. Caseous necrosis: Caseous necrosis is typically seen in granulomatous infections, such as tuberculosis. The necrotic tissue becomes dry and crumbly with a cheese-like appearance. This is not typically seen in abscess formation in the brain, which is associated with liquefactive necrosis rather than the characteristic appearance of caseous necrosis. B. Coagulative necrosis: Coagulative necrosis is the most common form of necrosis in ischemic injury (e.g., myocardial infarction). It involves the preservation of tissue architecture, although the cells lose their nuclei and eventually undergo breakdown. While coagulative necrosis is a hallmark of ischemia, it is not typically associated with abscesses, which tend to involve liquefactive necrosis. C. Fibrinoid necrosis: Fibrinoid necrosis refers to the deposition of fibrin-like material in blood vessel walls, often seen in immune complex diseases like vasculitis. This type of necrosis is associated with vascular damage and is not characteristic of abscess formation, which involves liquefactive necrosis of infected tissue.

questions.stem: After a football injury, a 16-year-old boy survives a ruptured spleen, hemorrhagic shock, and profound hypotension; however, a period of severe oliguria follows, so the boy undergoes a kidney biopsy.Which one of the following renal tubular changes found represents irreversible cellular injury?
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Answer (D)

Nuclear pyknosis, along with karyorrhexis and karyolysis, is a sign of necrosis and is, of course, irreversible. Fatty change, formation of cell blebs or myelin figures, and swelling of the cell or of organelles are all reversible changes. multiple myelin figures along with flocculent amorphous mitochondrial densities also indicate irreversible cell injury

questions.stem: All of the following are true about ferroptosis except

options.label: A
options.text: Ferroptosis is characterized by the accumulation of lipid peroxides

options.label: B
options.text: Ferroptosis is a form of regulated cell death that does not involve caspase activation

options.label: C
options.text: Ferroptosis is primarily triggered by mitochondrial dysfunction

options.label: D
options.text: Ferroptosis can be inhibited by iron chelators and antioxidants targeting lipid peroxidation

questions.answerText: Ferroptosis is primarily triggered by mitochondrial dysfunction
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) Ferroptosis is not primarily triggered by mitochondrial dysfunction, it is mainly caused by the accumulation of lipid peroxides and iron-dependent processes. Mitochondrial dysfunction is more central to other forms of cell death like apoptosis Other options: Ferroptosis is characterized by the accumulation of lipid peroxides, which are reactive molecules formed by oxidative damage to lipids, especially polyunsaturated fatty acids. This accumulation disrupts the cell membrane and is a hallmark of ferroptosis Ferroptosis is a regulated form of cell death that does not involve caspases, which distinguishes it from apoptosis. It is instead driven by oxidative damage and the dysregulation of iron homeostasis Ferroptosis can indeed be inhibited by iron chelators, which limit the availability of iron, and by antioxidants that target lipid peroxidation, such as glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), which neutralizes lipid peroxides and protects against ferroptosis

questions.stem: Which of the following is the correct sequence of nuclear changes observed during cell injury?
questions.solutionHtml:
/p>

Explanation of the Incorrect Options:

(A) Karyolysis → Pyknosis → Karyorrhexis:
This sequence is incorrect because karyolysis is the final stage of nuclear degradation, not the initial step. Nuclear dissolution (karyolysis) occurs after the nucleus undergoes condensation (pyknosis) and fragmentation (karyorrhexis). Starting with karyolysis misrepresents the progression of nuclear changes.

(C) Karyorrhexis → Karyolysis → Pyknosis:
This sequence is incorrect because karyorrhexis and karyolysis occur after pyknosis, not before. Pyknosis is the first step where the nucleus condenses, followed by fragmentation (karyorrhexis) and dissolution (karyolysis). Reversing this order does not align with the typical progression.

(D) Karyolysis → Karyorrhexis → Pyknosis:
This sequence is also incorrect because karyolysis is the final step, not the starting point. Nuclear condensation (pyknosis) must occur before fragmentation (karyorrhexis) and dissolution (karyolysis). Reversing the order disrupts the logical sequence of nuclear changes.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true about efferocytosis?

options.label: A
options.text: It involves the engulfment of apoptotic cells by macrophages

options.label: B
options.text: Efferocytosis leads to the activation of inflammation

options.label: C
options.text: It is a process that occurs only in the nervous system

options.label: D
options.text: Efferocytosis results in the production of reactive oxygen species

questions.answerText: It involves the engulfment of apoptotic cells by macrophages
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) Efferocytosis is the process in which macrophages or other phagocytic cells engulf and clear apoptotic cells. This is an essential process for maintaining tissue homeostasis and preventing the release of pro-inflammatory contents from dying cells Other options: Efferocytosis typically prevents inflammation, not activates it. By clearing apoptotic cells, it helps resolve inflammation and tissue damage rather than promoting further immune responses Efferocytosis is a process that occurs in multiple tissues and is not limited to the nervous system. It plays a key role in various organs and systems to maintain cellular homeostasis Efferocytosis does not typically lead to the production of reactive oxygen species. In fact, it helps prevent the release of ROS and other pro-inflammatory mediators by removing dying cells in an anti-inflammatory manner

questions.stem: All of the following are true about necroptosis except

options.label: A
options.text: MLKL (Mixed Lineage Kinase Domain-Like) plays a crucial role in the execution of necroptosis

options.label: B
options.text: Necroptosis is mediated by the activation of RIPK1 and RIPK3

options.label: C
options.text: Necroptosis results in the activation of caspases

options.label: D
options.text: Necroptosis leads to plasma membrane rupture and the release of cellular contents

questions.answerText: Necroptosis results in the activation of caspases
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) Necroptosis does not involve the activation of caspases, which are typically involved in apoptosis. This distinguishes necroptosis from apoptotic cell death, as it occurs through a caspase-independent pathway Other options: MLKL (Mixed Lineage Kinase Domain-Like protein) is crucial for executing necroptosis. Once phosphorylated by RIPK3, MLKL forms pores in the plasma membrane, leading to cell rupture and death Necroptosis is mediated by the activation of receptor-interacting protein kinases (RIPK1 and RIPK3), which play central roles in initiating the signalling cascade that leads to necroptosis Necroptosis leads to plasma membrane rupture and the release of cellular contents, like necrosis. This results in inflammation due to the leakage of cellular components into the extracellular space
